posts.caption:
Could you actually live car-light in the Arts District? Mostly for the fun part of the week.

What walks: the core is a handful of blocks along Main Street, roughly Charleston to Colorado. Park once and you can do coffee, lunch, a record shop, galleries and a bar on foot.

What doesn't: a full grocery run or big-box errands. A few blocks out, sidewalks get gappy, streets get wide and fast, and the shade disappears.

Living there means older lofts, condos, and new apartments going up on the edges. Parking gets tight on First Friday, and weekend nights get loud.

Car-light for Saturdays, not car-free. If that's the trade you want, it's worth a look.

posts.caption:
Two Las Vegas homes at the same price can carry very different monthly costs, and the difference usually isn't the mortgage.

HOA dues: many communities stack a master association and a sub-association; some have almost nothing. It varies by neighborhood far more than by area.

SIDs and LIDs: Special and Local Improvement Districts finance public infrastructure like streets, sidewalks, streetlights, sewer and water with bonds, repaid by the parcels that benefit. Clark County says special assessments are billed separately from property taxes, and an assessment is a lien on the property until it's paid off.

Before you commit to an address, get its HOA, master assessment, any SID/LID balance, and the tax that parcel will carry.

Send me an address and I'll help you find its numbers.

backups.title: The property tax on a listing may not be yours
backups.takeaway: Nevada's 3% cap is tied to the owner's primary-residence claim. When you buy, file your own.
backups.cta: Send me an address you're considering and I'll walk you through how the cap works for it before you offer.
backups.ctaNote: Manual service by Mikey. Nothing is automated.

slides.want: Nevada caps the tax bill increase on a primary residence at 3%.

slides.want: palm-lined street

slides.headline: So the seller's capped bill doesn't.

slides.want: So the seller's capped bill doesn't carry over.

slides.headline: Nevada law now puts a claim.
slides.want: Nevada law now puts a claim section on the Declaration of Value filed at closing.

backups.caption:
An easy budgeting mistake on a Las Vegas resale: trusting the tax number on the listing.

Nevada caps the annual increase on a primary residence's tax bill at 3% (NRS 361.4723). Homes that aren't owner-occupied can see up to 8%. The cap is tied to the owner's primary-residence claim: Clark County says any ownership document recorded removes the owner-occupied 3% abatement.

So the seller's capped bill doesn't simply carry over to you. Nevada law now requires a section on the Declaration of Value, filed with the deed at closing, where a new owner can claim it (NRS 375.060). The county also mails new owners a tax cap notice.

Before you trust a listing's tax figure, ask how the cap works for that exact property. Send me the address and I'll walk you through it.

backups.caption:
Moving this fall or winter? The cooler months are the time to check what your first Las Vegas summer will test.

The AC is a utility, not a luxury: get it serviced before summer hits its stride, because a system that struggles in June can fail outright by August. When you tour homes now, notice the shade: newer neighborhoods haven't grown into it yet, while established streets have real tree canopy. Ask what a home's AC, orientation and location mean day to day.

Next summer, cars turn into ovens fast, so never leave kids or pets in a parked car. And the part newcomers don't expect: the National Weather Service puts Southern Nevada's monsoon window at June 15 through September 30. Pull over in a dust storm, and never drive into water you can't see the bottom of.

People live full outdoor lives here every summer. They just move the schedule earlier.
